worked_solution:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -3}\frac{\sqrt{x+7}-2}{x+3} & =\frac{\sqrt{-3+7}-2}{-3+3}=\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the numerator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the numerator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -3}\frac{\sqrt{x+7}-2}{x+3} & ={lim}_{x\to -3}\frac{(\sqrt{x+7}-2)(\sqrt{x+7}+2)}{(x+3)(\sqrt{x+7}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -3}\frac{(\sqrt{x+7})^{2}-{2}^{2}}{(x+3)(\sqrt{x+7}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -3}\frac{(x+7)-4}{(x+3)(\sqrt{x+7}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -3}\frac{x+3}{(x+3)(\sqrt{x+7}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -3}\frac{\cancel{x+3}}{\cancel{(x+3)}(\sqrt{x+7}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -3}\frac{1}{\sqrt{x+7}+2} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{-3+7}+2} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{4}+2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2+2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$
